In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July.

Publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST.

“A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.”

O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week.

It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said.

Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski.

The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said.

Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

“We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”

Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July.

DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position.

But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site.

The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath.

Similarweb stats showed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said.

In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said.

In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.”

The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews.

Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.

#7284. Sumo Logic: Principal Product Marketing Manager

As a Principal Product Marketing Manager — AI Systems & Content Architecture, you will determine the architecture of our narrative and collateral engine. Rather than operating as an artisanal, bespoke content creator, your mandate is to establish our foundational positioning architecture and engineer high-leverage, AI-driven workflows that generate enterprise-grade sales collateral at scale. Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

A Thanksgiving roundup of eight search changes from this year worth a thank-you, from AI visibility data and social reports to a back button policy.

In SEO, we like to complain, but this industry and craft is also about finding the small wins to celebrate. Today is a day to consider what we are thankful for, so let us dig deep and create our SEO Thanksgiving list.

Search may have given us plenty to navigate this year in AI, but Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI were each able to find their own ways to offer up some AI visibility. We can take the crumbs.

This article is the Search Engine Journal Thanksgiving list for all things SEO, social, local, and PPC. We finish off with a celebration for anybody who clicked their back button and went somewhere they had never been before.

Google Search Console is currently displaying dedicated reports for your impressions in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and generative AI features in Discover, by page, country, and date. These new reports were released in June, and Google’s announcement now says, “As of August 31, 2026, we’ve rolled out these insights to all websites worldwide.”

We’re glad to finally see the AI impressions separated out from the normal impression totals.

SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide

Microsoft Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI performance report in February as a public preview, showing how many times Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summarizations, and some partner integrations reference your content, along with the referenced pages and the grounding query (the phrase used by the AI to retrieve the content).

In June, Microsoft added a Citation Share feature in preview, which provides insight into what percentage of citations for a grounding query go to your site. The February report gives you a count of how many times you appeared in the citation list, and Citation Share shows how large a piece of the pie those citations represent.

SEJ covered it here: Bing Webmaster Tools Adds AI Citation Performance Data and here Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide

On Nov. 10, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Business Hub in beta. All eligible businesses where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in Business Hub and, after claims and identity verification are approved, will be able to see mentions, website clicks, and discovery topics over the past 28 days.

According to OpenAI’s setup guide for online businesses, a mention occurs when ChatGPT references your website, not if it just names your brand.

Vahan Petrosyan, director of technology for SEJ, submitted Search Engine Journal, and Business Hub showed 353,356 mentions and 2,663 website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10.

SEJ’s mentions and website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10. Screenshot by Vahan Petrosyan, Search Engine Journal.

This is a beta version, and OpenAI says that claiming a business does not assure greater visibility within ChatGPT. However, these numbers are provided directly from ChatGPT, and mentions cannot be reflected in referral reports.

SEJ covered it here: How to Submit Your Website to ChatGPT Business Hub

Google introduced platform properties for social and video accounts in July and made them available to everybody worldwide on July 29. They provide information regarding clicks, impressions, CTR and average position for posts on Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube appearing in Google Search. Reports for Discover and Google News will also be displayed when applicable.

The Insights report for a YouTube platform property shows clicks from Google Search over 28 days. Source: Google Search Central (CC BY 4.0, cropped).

Your social team can now track how users locate the team’s social content on Google Search, within Search Console, the same tool utilized by your SEO team.

SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console Adds Reports For Social Posts

Google announced the branded queries filter last November and made it available to all eligible sites by March. The branded queries filter allows you to sort your Performance report queries into branded, including misspellings, and non-branded, so you can identify traffic coming from users searching specifically for your brand or products.

The Search Analytics API got the same branded split this month. Prior to this branded queries filter being implemented, tracking traffic based upon specific branded searches required “maintaining complex keyword regex lists,” as Google put it. Many will agree that it is refreshing to no longer need such lists.

SEJ covered it here: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API

Google’s September Small Business Bulletin described view counts for Business Profile posts as “currently rolling out globally.”

Once the rollout has completed for your Business Profile, each post card located under the dashboard section will indicate views generated from Search and Maps activity for posts from the past 18 months.

Google removed post metrics from Business Profiles in 2023. Now you can determine which posts receive the most views rather than making educated guesses. However, the bulletin said the counts were not accessible via the API yet.

SEJ covered it here: Google Adds Post View Counts To Business Profiles

For PPC advertisers working in TikTok Ads Manager, the Q4 product preview highlighted Impression Share, a common metric seen in Google Ads, along with Top 1 Impression Share for Search Ads campaigns.

Impression Share measures the percentage of eligible search results impressions that your ads capture. According to TikTok’s help section, availability of Impression Share may vary depending on account and market. Still, it can quickly reveal what portion of eligible search visibility you are leaving behind.

TikTok also added Keyword Packs (pre-made brand and category keywords) to the Keyword Suggestion Tool for a faster way to create keyword lists.

SEJ covered it here: TikTok Search Ads Adds Brand And Category Keyword Packs

Google began treating back button hijacking as a malicious practice in April and started enforcing this policy on June 15. Sites using back button hijacking could be subject to either a manual action or automated demotion.

On Nov. 23, Google released a new FAQ which says the policy will apply if the back button hijacking occurs in a user’s browser, including when they visit your page via social media. Although this policy cannot eliminate all cases of back button hijacking, websites currently utilizing this tactic may want to stop.

SEJ covered it here: Google Says Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits

Our single request for next year’s Thanksgiving holiday is the ability to differentiate Search Console’s AI clicks from web clicks. Currently, every time someone clicks on an AI Overview or AI Mode link, that click counts in the same Performance report as clicks on your other search engine results.

Happy Thanksgiving from all the SEJ team.

#7282. The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.

Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.

The Nov. 18 disclosure raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of CTV ad fraud detection — and how much fraudulent inventory slips through existing safeguards, important gaps for the industry to collectively plug as marketers increasingly spend ad dollars on such channels.

According to HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence team, the situation involved a network of compromised, low-cost Android-based streaming devices running malware designed to generate fraudulent video advertising activity without their owners’ knowledge.

The operation was more than three times larger, by peak daily bid-request volume, than VASTFLUX, previously the largest publicly disclosed scheme measured on that basis.

Researchers linked elements of the malware distribution infrastructure to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, identifying connections involving device software, code repositories and command-and-control servers.

HUMAN also uncovered links to earlier BADBOX operations, including BADBOX 2.0, which was exposed in 2025 and involved more than 10 million compromised devices across 222 countries and territories.

The latest discovery illustrates how fraud operations can reconstitute themselves following earlier disruptions, adapting their infrastructure and techniques to evade detection.

The malware then installed advertising software on infected devices, allowing video commercials to play in hidden windows while users continued watching television or navigating their streaming interfaces.

The resulting advertising requests impersonated legitimate CTV applications, making the inventory appear authentic to downstream buyers.

Some fraudulent requests also originated from residential proxy networks, helping disguise their source as ordinary household internet traffic.

HUMAN identified 11 proxy networks in which compromised devices could be enrolled without their owners’ consent, effectively turning consumer internet connections into infrastructure available for third-party use. Separately, researchers uncovered spoofed server-side ad insertion traffic, in which fraudulent requests purported to represent advertisements inserted into streaming sessions that did not actually exist.

The scale of the operation is considerable, although its financial impact remains unclear.

Crucially, the 40 billion figure represents bid requests, not completed advertising transactions or billable impressions. Consequently, it cannot be used to calculate advertiser losses without establishing how much fraudulent inventory was purchased.

Hence, the question remains: what proportion of the 40 billion daily bid requests became paid impressions? And how much money was spent on invalid inventory?

However, due to the intricacies of online ad auctions – where CPMs can vary significantly – HUMAN was unable to provide an exact dollar amount when asked about the financial impact of the operation.

Nonetheless, sources approached by Digiday estimated that BADBOX 3.0 could potentially have cost advertisers millions of dollars per day at its height.

Shailin Dhar, partner at Futureproof TMT, cautioned against equating the operation’s 40 billion daily bid requests with actual advertiser losses, noting that CTV supply audited by his firm since 2024 has averaged a fill rate of approximately 2%. He further counseled that fraudulent inventory originating from low-end applications and devices could perform considerably worse.

At this juncture, it’s worth considering that enormous volumes of fraudulent auction traffic do not necessarily translate into equivalent volumes of wasted advertising expenditure. At an illustrative fill rate of 0.5% and realized revenue of $3 per thousand impressions, 40 billion daily requests would generate approximately $600,000 in revenue. However, Dhar stressed that such calculations should not be mistaken for evidence of the operation’s actual earnings.

Nevertheless, the operation’s ability to masquerade as legitimate streaming inventory highlights potential weaknesses in how CTV advertising transactions are authenticated.

CTV has become an increasingly important channel for advertisers seeking to reach audiences migrating from traditional television. However, its programmatic infrastructure also presents opportunities for fraudsters to exploit fragmented supply paths and inconsistent verification practices.

BADBOX 3.0 demonstrates how apparently legitimate app identifiers, residential IP addresses and video ad requests can be combined to manufacture the appearance of genuine viewing activity. The question is whether existing safeguards can consistently identify such behavior before advertisers are charged.

Futureproof’s Dhar questioned the effectiveness of existing verification safeguards, arguing that private marketplaces and curated deals remain vulnerable because of limited device, content, and connection signals, alongside excessive confidence in identity matching.

“My personal estimate is roughly a 90% chance that at least one comparable operation is running without public identification,” he told Digiday, while acknowledging that its scale and financial impact remain unknown.

Per Dhar’s assessment, effective CTV verification requires persistent checks throughout the advertising supply chain, rather than relying exclusively on pre-bid or post-bid detection.

For now, HUMAN says customers using its Ad Fraud Defense service are protected against the operation’s associated attacks, while its researchers continue monitoring the perpetrators for further adaptations.

The findings come roughly a month after a separate investigation by ad security firm Confiant and researchers at Citizen Lab exposed how online advertising infrastructure was used to distribute spyware, highlighting another vulnerability in the digital advertising ecosystem.

That investigation, detailed in research published by Citizen Lab, found that Israeli company Discover-Tech exploited targeted advertising mechanisms to deliver zero-click spyware, including attacks against devices at Al Jazeera.

While the two operations differed in their objectives — one targeting advertising budgets, the other facilitating surveillance — both illustrate how infrastructure designed to connect advertisers with audiences can be repurposed for malicious activity.

The broader concern is that BADBOX 3.0 is another iteration of an established threat rather than an isolated incident — and that dismantling one operation does not necessarily eliminate the infrastructure or incentives behind the next.

FutureSight’s new tool can help banks of all sizes get a side-by-side idea of how their media mix stacks up against the competition.

Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

Hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

We are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

You will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling new features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

Experience at a SaaS or software product company, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

Threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

You read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

You build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

Clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

Willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

#7280. Confident kids, cautious elders: What we get wrong (and right) about who really understands social media algorithms

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

RELATED ARTICLETrapped by what they know: Young adults’ algorithmic cynicismMyojung ChungNovember 17, 2025In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in New Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

The self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

In other words, the generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

To capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

Then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

Exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger users, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

My data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

This miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It shows up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

RELATED ARTICLEWant to fight misinformation? Teach people how algorithms workMyojung ChungSeptember 4, 2024Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

Other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

But the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident users, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.

Third, anyone trying to reach audiences through algorithmic platforms, from educators to newsrooms to the platforms themselves, should stop assuming that the youngest users are the savviest. Confidence and competence are different things, and treating one as a proxy for the other leaves both groups poorly served.

The next time a young adult confidently explains “how the algorithm works,” it might be worth asking: How can you be sure you actually know that? And the next time an older relative shrugs and says they don’t think they get it, it might be just another kind of miscalibration — with costs of its own, just a quieter one.

Myojung Chung is an associate professor of journalism and media innovation at Northeastern University and a faculty associate at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University.

#7278. The Wall Street Journal joins a growing list of publishers disallowing bots by default

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Many publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.

One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

As part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

“As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” said Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”

The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent company, News Corp.

“We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”

Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents shows that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

Many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the company’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

“One of the most important issues for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”

More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

People Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

Many of these publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

Despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The company started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

Known Agents currently tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

“Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” said King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”

King acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

“It’s been such a manual process,” said King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”

Slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the company’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

“We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, said. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”

Lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he said.

Slate currently has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

“It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” said Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [update your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”

#7275. D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →

This is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies. The report is based on a survey of 90 brand and retailer professionals, as well as individual interviews with marketing executives.

Digiday’s survey found that brands and retailers plan to adjust the marketing tactics they’ll use during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to those they used in 2025.

The biggest changes are that CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026, with year-over-year increases of 22 percentage points and 20 percentage points, respectively.

Forty-five percent of survey respondents said they plan to use CTV/streaming ads this holiday season, in comparison to 23% of respondents who said the same in 2025. The 2026 uptick followed a 14 percentage point dip in usage from 2024 to 2025.Meanwhile, marketers’ usage of TV ads remained relatively stable between 2024 and 2025, dropping by only 4 percentage points between 2024 and 2025, but grew by a whopping 20 percentage points in 2026. Thirty-three percent of brands and retailers said they plan to use TV ads this holiday season in comparison to 13% of marketers who said the same in 2025.

“Streaming is a really valid channel to invest in during holiday because consumption of that media spikes,” said Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement company Ritual. “But participating in streaming is actually a decision for the whole year. Starting to engage just for holiday would be a risky move, especially for a smaller brand.”

“If you have the data to back it up over the course of the year showing this is a channel that’s proven and the ROI metrics associated, it can make a lot of sense to spike it during holiday,” she added.

Ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, said that both streaming and TV ads can be effective for targeting specific demographic groups during the holidays. “Streaming and television is an effective audience conversion mechanism, especially with women over 30 years old,” Bloom said. “We’ve done a lot of work on daytime TV and on QVC. We see significantly bigger segments in the holiday time period from November through mid-December, and we always put attention on those times.”

Last year, brands’ and retailers’ most-used holiday marketing tactic was brand experiences, but that strategy fell to second place in 2026 behind streaming/CTV ads. Forty-one percent of marketers said they expect to use brand experiences as a marketing strategy during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to 50% of marketers who said the same in 2025 — a drop of 9 percentage points.

Brands and retailers are also divesting from using gift guides and influencer hauls/unboxing videos this holiday season. Marketers’ usage of gift guides decreased by 19 percentage points in 2026 vs. 2025, while their use of influencer hauls/unboxing videos fell by 14 percentage points this year in comparison to last year.

Although gift guides and brand experiences decreased in marketer usage for the 2026 holidays, they remain brands’ and retailers’ top performing holiday marketing tactics over time. Thirty-one percent of marketers said gift guides have historically performed the best for their company during the holiday season, while 28% of marketers said the same of brand experiences, putting them in the No. 1 and No. 2 ranking spots, respectively.

Although some marketers are shifting away from using gift guides for the upcoming holiday season, Ritual’s Brodie said gift guides are likely to gain importance in the AI-driven search era because AI-powered search tools often rely on best of lists and curated recommendations to answer consumer queries.

“Gift guides are very interesting in the world of AEO and thinking about LLM optimization,” Brodie said. “Overall, best of lists and gift guides are a close sister to [AI search results]. Gift guides can play an important role in holiday and especially bridging LLM research and AI overviews. So, I’m bullish about gift guides.”

Although brands and retailers are leaning into CTV/streaming ads for the 2026 holidays, those marketing tactics tied in the No. 4 spot for the best-performing holiday marketing tactic over time, while pop-up shops ranked No. 3. Influencer hauls/unboxing videos was the only marketing strategy that fell in both best historic performance and marketers’ intended use during the 2026 holiday season.

A-Frame Brands’ Bloom said brands and retailers should also consider investing in catalogs for the 2026 holiday. “Catalogs have always been very successful, and they’re heavily conversion-focused,” Bloom explained. “When they’re discount-driven and when people’s attention is on buying, you can do offers that you can only get via physical paper, and it does drive people into stores.”

As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

#7274. The Missing Step In Prompt Tracking Was Written Down In 1995 via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Prompt tracking has no method for choosing prompts or defining a correct answer. Competency questions, a 1995 knowledge engineering method, fill that gap.

The AI visibility industry has worked out how many prompts to track and how often to run them, and it still has no method for deciding which questions belong in the set or what a correct answer to any of them would be. That second problem is older than the first, and it has a documented solution that predates Google. Knowledge engineers have used it since the mid-1990s under the name competency questions, and it is almost absent from the conversation in search.

Over the last year, the sampling side of prompt tracking has matured quickly. Practitioners now broadly accept that a single run of a single prompt tells you very little, that branded and unbranded prompts have to be reported separately, and that wording changes results. The research supports the caution. A peer-reviewed study presented at ICLR 2024 found that formatting changes alone, with the meaning of the prompt untouched, moved one open-source model’s accuracy by as much as 76 points on standard benchmark tasks. That study tested benchmarks, not brands, but it establishes the underlying behavior: These systems respond to the form of a question as well as its content.

What has not matured is the step before sampling. A scoping review posted this fall examined 38 empirical studies that query language models and measure outcomes for brands, and it judged that only five of them could defend how their prompts were chosen. Most used prompts written by the authors or generated by a model, with no evidence that those prompts represent what buyers ask. A separate survey makes the consequence plain: the prompts you pick, and the weight you give each one, define the market your visibility score describes, and that market may not match real demand. Both papers are preprints from single authors and have not been through peer review, so I treat them as a careful reading of the field and not as final findings.

The same review found that authors with a commercial stake in visibility services, or in a brand being measured, were behind 19 of those 38 studies. I am one of those people, since I founded CitationIQ, which measures AI visibility, and you should weigh what follows with that understanding (I was not part of any of those studies, for the record).

The practical result is familiar to anyone who has sat in a prompt-selection meeting or had to choose them. Someone opens a spreadsheet, the team brainstorms questions, a tool suggests a few hundred more, and the list is frozen so that next month’s number can be compared with this month’s. Nobody writes down why each prompt is there, what business situation it stands for, or what the model would have to say for the answer to count as right. The score that comes out is precise, and its meaning is undefined.

In the early 1990s, Michael Grüninger and Mark Fox at the University of Toronto were building formal models of how enterprises operate, and they needed a way to decide what a model had to contain before anyone built it. Their answer, published in 1995, was to start with the situations the model had to support and then write the questions it must be able to answer in those situations. They called these competency questions because the questions define what the model is competent to do.

The thing they were building is called an ontology, which is easiest to relate to the knowledge graph you already know. The graph holds the facts, and the ontology is the plan those facts are organized by: what kinds of things exist, what properties they carry, and how they can relate. Schema.org plays that role for structured data on the web. Most entity work fills in the graph without stating what it must be able to answer, which is the gap competency questions close. From here on I will call the ontology a knowledge model.

A competency question is a question a knowledge model must be able to answer, written down before the model is built and used afterward to test whether it works. The questions come first, they come from real situations, and they double as the acceptance test. The Toronto method ran in six stages: Describe the motivating scenarios, write the questions informally, define the terms, restate the questions formally, write the rules, and then establish the conditions under which the model answers the questions completely. Later researchers borrowed test-first development from software engineering and turned the questions into tests that are written before the model is changed.

Set that beside the spreadsheet. The knowledge engineer can trace every question to a scenario and every test to a question. The prompt list has no scenarios behind it and no expected answers in front of it.

It would be convenient to say that knowledge engineers solved this and marketers only need to copy them, and it would be wrong. A 2023 survey of 63 ontology engineers found that most of them use competency questions routinely, and that 77.8% have difficulty making sure their questions are both necessary and sufficient. Nearly two-thirds have trouble identifying questions that truly represent the scope, about half have trouble writing them properly, and two-thirds work with no guideline at all. Other researchers note that teams rarely publish their questions alongside the finished model, which means the requirements are often lost.

I find that reassuring, not discouraging. Thirty years of practice has produced a clear record of where the method breaks: vague questions, questions nobody can check, question sets that drift away from the scenarios that justified them, and requirements that live in one person’s head. Those are the failures a prompt list has today, and the knowledge engineering literature has names and partial remedies for each of them. One recent classification separates scoping questions, which mark out what a model should cover, from validating questions, which check whether what it says is correct. That split maps directly onto the two things a brand wants to know: whether it appears in the answer at all, and whether what the answer says about it is true.

The method does not transfer whole, and the reason matters. A knowledge model is deterministic: you run the formal query, and it returns the answer, or it does not. A language model is probabilistic, so the same question produces different answers across runs, phrasings, and engines, and the result is a rate instead of a pass or fail. You also do not own the thing being tested. A knowledge engineer who finds a failed question fixes the model, while you can only change the material the model draws on.

My adaptation, which is my own extension and not something the literature prescribes, is to run each competency question as two tests in a fixed order. First test your own content, which is deterministic: can a person find the expected answer, stated plainly, on a page you control or in a source you can influence? That is a pass or a fail, and you can fix a fail yourself. Only then test the language model by asking the question in several phrasings, several times, across the engines your buyers use, and recording how often the expected answer comes back. A critical survey of GEO research recommends three to five phrasings per information need, which is a sensible floor.

The order matters because a language model that fails a question your own content cannot answer has told you nothing about the language model. In an earlier piece, I argued that AI visibility is three separate problems on three layers, and this is the diagnostic step that tells you which layer to look at. It also clarifies the relationship between a question and a prompt. The competency question is the requirement and the prompts are test cases for it, so twenty phrasings of one question are still one requirement, and a list of three hundred prompts may cover far fewer needs than it appears to.

To make this concrete, take DuaneRoll, a payroll software company I invented for this article. It sells to businesses with 50 to 500 employees, and its motivating scenario is a finance leader whose company has just hired in a third state and who asks an AI assistant what to do about payroll. Here are five competency questions for it.

The fifth question is the one most prompt lists lack. An AI answer that credits you with a service you do not offer creates a support problem at best, and as I wrote about the German court rulings, an answer built from accurate facts attached to the wrong company can become a legal one. Testing for what should not be said is as much a requirement as testing for what should.

Notice what the bad question has in common with most tracked prompts. It sounds like something a buyer would ask, it produces an answer every time, and the answer can be scored for sentiment. It fails as a requirement because there is nothing to check it against.

Every expected answer above has a named owner, and that is deliberate. In knowledge engineering, a domain expert stands behind each expected answer. A prompt test usually has no such person, and the result gets pasted into a report with no record of which model, which version, which date, or whether web search was on. Sascha Donner, writing this year in the Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, argues that text from a language model lacks the testimonial grounding documents have always had, and that it becomes a usable document only when a person fixes it in a form and takes responsibility for it. The same applies to a test result. An expected answer needs a witness, meaning a named person who will say it is correct, and a logged result needs its conditions recorded, or it is an anecdote with a percentage attached.

Once the questions exist, most of the measurement decisions make themselves. Each question says what to look for, each expected answer says what counts as correct, each owner says who to ask when the answer changes, and each scenario says why the question deserves a place in the set. Sampling, which the industry has learned to do well, then operates on a set that means something. A score built that way can be explained to a chief marketing officer in one sentence: Of the things buyers need to know about us, this is the share the engines get right.

One caution before you hand the job to a machine. Asking an AI system to write your competency questions and grade the answers is tempting, and researchers are actively studying it. A study using 1,393 competency questions found that human evaluators’ performance dropped when the AI assistant gave them incorrect guidance. A language model can draft candidate questions quickly, and a person who knows the business still has to decide which ones are requirements.

A competency question set for a brand is a short, owned list of what buyers must be able to learn about you, each item traceable to a real buying situation and paired with an answer someone will vouch for. Start with 10. Write the scenario, the question, the expected answer, and the owner; check your own content first, and only then look at what the engines say. The method is thirty years old, its weaknesses are well documented, and it is still more than most prompt lists have behind them.

#7271. Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Amol Waishampayan, co-founder, fullthrottle.ai

Agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story. Faster work, leaner teams, lower fees. Clients took the meeting, nodded along and then waited for the invoice to shrink. It didn’t. AI strategies now sound interchangeable to clients, who say the savings never showed up in their fees.

That is not an AI problem. It is a positioning problem. Efficiency was the wrong promise. Clients do not hire agencies to be fast. They hire them to grow the business. AI’s real opportunity for agencies is not doing the same work cheaper. It is doing work that actually moves revenue, and proving it.

Agencies are getting operational value from AI. According to the Digiday Media Agency Report 2026, 70% of agencies say AI has cut costs by making tasks more efficient, while 31% say it cost more to implement than expected. But efficiency is a one-time gain.

Once every agency has it, nobody gets paid for it. As one Gartner analyst told Digiday, the honeymoon between agencies and AI is “essentially over.” The agencies that build their AI story on productivity are competing on margin. The ones that build it on performance are competing on value, and value is what clients renew.

Most media plans are still organized by channel. Search budget here, social budget there, streaming over in a separate deck. AI makes that structure obsolete, because it can plan around the customer instead.

Take a regional home services company running paid search and social. Those campaigns are producing something more valuable than clicks: a live stream of households actively researching its services. AI can turn those signals into a defined first-party audience, figure out where else those households spend their time, and extend the plan into streaming TV, digital video and audio to reach them there. One audience, coordinated across channels, built from the client’s own demand rather than a platform’s inventory.

That is a different kind of planning. The question stops being “what should we spend on CTV” and becomes “who are we trying to reach, and where are they?”

The next step is letting AI act on that intelligence. Agentic systems can take audience and performance signals and adjust targeting, channel mix and spend as conditions change, instead of waiting for the monthly optimization meeting. Static plans with quarterly reviews are a relic of how long it used to take humans to read the data.

But here is where agencies should be careful. The advantage is not how much of the buying you automate. Anyone can automate. The advantage is whether the agent is optimizing toward something that matters. An agent chasing cheaper CPMs will find them, and the client will not care. An agent optimizing toward the client’s actual business outcomes, with the agency keeping full transparency and control, is a different product entirely.

This is the part most of the industry still avoids. Clicks and impressions are easy to report and nearly impossible to defend in a budget conversation. The only metrics a CFO cares about are sales, customers and revenue.

Once that loop exists, everything upstream improves. Planning gets smarter because it is fed by real conversions. Agentic buying gets better because it is optimizing toward revenue instead of proxies. And the agency walks into every renewal with proof rather than a deck.

Agencies are already monetizing AI. Digiday’s report found that 59% are launching new AI-powered products, 34% are selling strategic roadmaps or audits and 31% are charging additional fees for AI-powered services. But if the product is “we have AI,” the pricing power will not last. Every competitor has AI. Within a year, every client will have it too.

The agencies that win the next cycle will not be the ones with the most AI. They will be the ones who can show a client exactly what it delivered, in the client’s own numbers. Efficiency gets agencies a thank-you. Outcomes get agencies the next three years of the account.Partner insights from fullthrottle.ai

#7270. Campaign Trail: Tiffany tells human holiday story with Hollywood talent

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The luxury brand and agency American Haiku leaned into real emotions with actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

In adland, it has been a decidedly handmade holiday season, with brands including Levi’s and E.l.f. turning to techniques like stop-motion animation to connect with consumers who are growing weary of ads created by artificial intelligence.

For its annual holiday effort, Tiffany & Co. found the best way to resonate with consumers is through human storytelling. The luxury brand’s global campaign, “Love is a Gift,” was created with agency American Haiku and revolves around a two-minute film starring actor Amanda Seyfried and director Derek Cianfrance.

The short, “You & Me,” jumps from the present day to New York City in the 1990s to tell the story of a young girl and her mother, played by Seyfried. The girl watches her mother work as a choreographer and has a handful of holiday experiences before being gifted with a Tiffany ornament that she shares with her own daughter in the present.

“Moving between past and present, the film reflects the enduring place Tiffany & Co. holds in life’s most meaningful moments and the stories we carry forward,” said CMO Andrea Davey in a statement.

The film is soundtracked by a cover of The Wannadies’ “You & Me Song,” a tune best known for its appearance on the 1996 “Romeo + Juliet” soundtrack. The campaign will run across cinema, paid and organic social, digital out-of-home, owned channels and clienteling across global channels.

Along with being on-trend with regard to stories imbued with humanity, Tiffany’s holiday campaign also represents a pivot from the brand’s past holiday creative. The 2025 edition of the “Love is a Gift” campaign turned its iconic blue boxes into portals to love stories around the world. This year, Tiffany brought on American Haiku, which had worked on a previous campaign for the brand in the U.K., but didn’t offer a traditional brief.

“They came to us with an initial idea of a family spending the holidays in their home and [tapping] into the memory aspect,” said Ben Muckensturm, creative director at the shop. “Where we pushed the work was bringing in the importance of the mother-daughter relationship that I think is the core of the story.”

Keying into the mother-daughter story gave the brand and agency a larger insight around the memory of seeing a parent as a person in their own world that is relatable to consumers, whether or not they are wealthy residents of the Upper East Side like the characters in the film. In the film, the true gift is not the ornament but the memory that is associated with it.

“That opened us up to how we explore the past and then bring it back to the present and create a piece that feels essentially real, that anyone could connect with,” Muckensturm said. “Everything was shot in New York. It was definitely an intentional push to try to bring it to the real world and make it more of an emotional piece.”

“You & Me” also delivers nostalgia for a pre-digital ‘90s that has been a reliable way to engage millennial audiences. However, the nostalgia in the film is not the traditional touchstones, like technology and boy bands, used by marketers looking to tap into memories of the decade. Instead, Tiffany looked at its own archives and at the holidays of movies like “Home Alone” and “The Parent Trap” for inspiration.

“When we created the town house, we went back to old archival Tiffany imagery of how things were,” Muckensturm said of creating the main set for the ad. “Especially on Fifth Avenue, most of the references that we brought were from ‘Home Alone 2,’ like what the streets looked like at the time. It's great to be able to tap into things that people are familiar with.”

After creating the world of the ad, the agency populated it with brand ambassador Seyfried, whose character is the mother in the past, rather than the main character in the present-day framing device. The actor, an Academy Award nominee whose performance in one of the year’s biggest films has captivated audiences, brought her gifts to the production.

“She has such a maternal instinct that really played perfectly on set, and you could see really how she was a mother to that girl for the days that we shot,” Muckensturm said.

The choice of Cianfrance, a director best known for dramatic fare like “Blue Valentine” and “The Place Beyond the Pines,” helped the brand and agency get the emotional tone right, without rehearsal and without falling into familiar or even corny holiday tropes.

“There was a trusting relationship between production partners, us and the client to come into it with a really open mind to see what the scene gives us,” Muckensturm said. “We knew where we were going to shoot, and we were trying to get a range of emotion… but we really let him direct them and let this play naturally.”

At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve. In the last six years, we've become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We’re also quickly scaling an injury practice to help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

So far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews. And we're just getting started.

We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, GV (Google Ventures), and True Ventures, with ambitions to create a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

Each month, tens of thousands of Americans seek our help for a single legal matter – applying for Social Security Disability, filing a Workers’ Compensation claim – but many of these clients are actually eligible for additional aid without ever knowing it.

Your job as Lead Attorney, New Verticals is to help us do right by these clients, helping them claim additional benefits through the social safety net. You’ll oversee the team of intake specialists who speak with clients who have secondary claims, evaluating the case facts and whether to connect them with an Atticus attorney or local attorney to provide legal advice and potentially take on their case.

This is a job that straddles the line between practicing the law and growing a business. It requires developing a strong understanding of multiple fields of law, and being able to accurately identify when we can help and when we cannot. But even more importantly, this job requires you to be an incredibly strong operator: you need to keep the big picture in mind and stay laser-focused on how we can achieve our goals, oftentimes finding outside-the-box ways to accomplish them. You will report to our General Manager of New Verticals and work closely with our CEO and Managing Attorney.

Speaking with severely injured clients trying to rebuild their lives after a catastrophic accident

This is a rare opportunity for an attorney to join a profitable and growing public-interest law firm and take on one of our biggest priorities as a company.

You can understand the nuances of various contingency fields of law and can apply them to a variety of cases (including Social Security Disability, Workers’ Compensation, Personal Injury, and more) – you don’t need to be an expert today, but you should be a fast learner.

You can empathize with anyone and quickly build rapport and relationships while exercising good judgment, both with our clients and local counsel at law firms across the country.

You have strong instincts and judgment as an operator – you can run effective and efficient processes, and you don’t let them run you.

#7266. The next test for agentic media

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory

Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work. These teams have their own agents, their own data and their own rules for what an agent may and may not do. At the same time, most of the specialized intelligence they depend on still sits inside separate vendor platforms.

As a result, vendor intelligence shapes a recommendation while remaining disconnected from the system acting on the recommendation. When planners carry conclusions between tools, the evidence and conditions behind those recommendations often fall away.

That’s the problem agentic media has to solve next. Can the intelligence behind the agent go where the work happens?

Models and agent frameworks are widely available. Two vendors can build on the same foundation and ship agents that look identical in a demo. What separates them is what the agent knows, and whether the advertiser can put that knowledge to work. In media buying, that knowledge is specific.

A broad content classification offers only a starting point for a media decision. Suitability depends on the particular advertiser and market, and those judgments can change quickly when breaking news alters the significance of a placement. A general-purpose model can’t reconstruct that brand-specific knowledge or historical context from a prompt alone. Classification depth and performance history can.

For Channel Factory, that means IAB 3.0 classification across more than 15 million YouTube channels, and more than 10 years and $4 billion of campaign performance data. To be clear, this isn’t an argument for keeping that intelligence locked inside a platform; it’s the opposite. Intelligence that only works inside its owner’s interface is as limited as a capable agent no one can reach.

So the test is portability. Can an advertiser’s own agent call on a provider’s intelligence directly, from inside the planning and buying environment it already uses? That’s how Channel Factory is building, with contextual and suitability intelligence made available through APIs and MCP servers, and delivered through modular agents that run inside an advertiser’s environment or alongside it.

With this architecture, market-specific suitability analysis becomes part of an advertiser’s own planning process. An agent can evaluate inventory against the provider’s classifications and historical performance data, applying the relevant standards for each market. Those findings can directly inform the plan, with the advertiser’s existing rules governing what the agent can recommend or change.

Portable intelligence doesn’t mean identical agents. Two advertisers can draw on the same underlying intelligence and make different decisions. For instance, one avoids content when signals are unclear while another favors reaching inside defined boundaries. Both are valid because the thresholds, priorities and approval rules are the advertisers’.

An agent’s knowledge source shouldn’t determine the scope of its authority. The brand decides what acceptable judgment looks like. The provider keeps the classification, history and models current.

Learning needs the same discipline. Feedback and outcomes should refine recommendations, but advertisers should decide what shapes future decisions and which policies stay fixed. On its own, a successful campaign shouldn’t rewrite a brand’s suitability standards.

Intelligence that moves into someone else’s systems has to carry its accountability along. As agents shift from recommending to acting, teams need to see what changed, why and whether it stayed within approved limits.

The principle is simple: Agents do the reasoning, and the engine owns the state, so every action is authorized, logged and traceable to the signals behind it. People define the strategy. Autonomy is earned in stages: alerts first, then recommendations, then bounded actions. An agent might make a small budget adjustment under set conditions while sending a larger change for human approval. How much authority to delegate is the advertiser’s call, and the system should make that call easy to enforce and easy to review.

As agentic capabilities spread, feature lists will converge. Advertisers should look underneath the interface and put three questions to any provider:

The providers who can answer those clearly will matter more as brands take greater control of how they buy media. The rest will be unrealized demos.

#7265. How Jell-O’s new creative platform looks to shift consumer perceptions

Let Marketing Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The campaign, the first by Johannes Leonardo for the Kraft Heinz brand, represents its largest marketing investment in more than a decade.

Jell-O on Monday launched a new creative platform, “Oh Hello, Jell-O,” that seeks to shift consumer perceptions about how the product can be enjoyed beyond traditional use cases. The effort represents the Kraft Heinz brand’s largest marketing investment in more than a decade, per details shared with Marketing Dive.

“As a nearly 130-year-old brand, we recognized a disconnect between how familiar consumers are with Jell-O and how often they think to purchase it,” Kathryn O’Brien, head of marketing for desserts at Kraft Heinz, said in emailed comments. “We want Jell-O to be more than something that comes to mind for a bowl of gelatin or pudding, but rather a part of the creative process in the kitchen.”

Central to the campaign are two 15-second spots that show home cooks in monochrome kitchens preparing desserts with Jell-O before a social-inspired flip transition pivots the scene to others marveling over the finished product.

The campaign was created by Johannes Leonardo and is the first campaign for the brand by the agency, which has held creative duties on select Kraft Heinz brands since 2020. The spots were directed by Drew Kirsch, a veteran of music videos who has worked with Taylor Swift, and feature an original electronic-pop song that uses “oh hello, Jell-O” as a vocal hook.

“Rather than borrowing an existing song, we saw an opportunity to build an ownable sonic identity around the platform,” O’Brien said. “The original track is a recognizable brand asset that can extend across social, content and future campaign moments.”

As part of the launch, Jell-O will take over the Las Vegas Sphere this week, transforming the orb into a gelatin mold, a “dirt cup” dessert and banana cream pudding. “Oh Hello, Jell-O” will run across streaming, online video, social and digital throughout 2027, with investment pulsing around key seasonal moments. The significant media investment comes at a pivotal moment for the brand, O’Brien explained.

“Our first-ever CTV buy allows us to bring the campaign's highly visual, music-driven creative to life on the big screen, showcasing the playfulness, vibrant colors and unexpected transformations in a high-attention environment,” the executive said. “We're taking an integrated approach throughout 2027, combining streaming and online video with social, digital and e-commerce touchpoints.”

The creative platform builds on a 2023 rebrand, crafted with agency Brand Opus, that updated Jell-O’s visual identity with a more modern look and feel. The rebrand, which at the time was its first such effort in 10 years, arrived amid an industry-wide move to help CPG brands engage with new consumer groups.

Kraft Heinz in February stopped plans to split its condiment and grocery staples businesses, with CEO Steve Cahillane saying many of the CPG company’s challenges are fixable. The company is pouring $700 million into a turnaround strategy that includes significant investments in marketing, which has been increased to at least 6% of net sales.

While Kraft Heinz saw organic net sales decrease 1.1% in Q3 2026, the company’s market share, sales and volume trends improved in every region, per an earnings report. Jell-O was cited on an earnings call as a brand with which the company is looking to win share by investing selectively.
